land.text: Judea around Jerusalem, with Jaffa and Gezer, whose independence Demetrius II recognised in 142 BCE (Simon Thassi page); the Acra in Jerusalem stayed a Seleucid fortress until 142/141

predecessors.note: Cliopatria draws a Judea shape from -144; the pages date independence to 142 (Simon Thassi), '142/141' (Hasmonean dynasty), 141 (Judea page timeline).

land.text: 'Judea, Samaria, and Idumea came under direct Roman administration' as the province of Judaea in 6 CE (Judaea page), with the Beersheba country as the south of Idumea; its capital was Caesarea Maritima

successors.note: Archelaus was deposed in 6 CE. The tetrarchies of Antipas (Galilee, Peraea; to 39 CE) and Philip (Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Paneas; to 34 CE) had split off in 4 BCE and are not Judea's successors.

capitals.name: Jerusalem
capitals.note: Hasmonean dynasty infobox: capital Jerusalem, historic seat Modi'in; Herodian kingdom infobox also gives Jerusalem.

capitals.name: Caesarea Maritima
capitals.note: Judea page timeline: 'c. 25 BCE: Caesarea Maritima is built by Herod the Great, replacing Jerusalem as the capital'; the Judaea (Roman province) infobox gives Caesarea. The Herodian kingdom page still gives Jerusalem, so the move is the Judea page's reading.

rulers.name: Simon Thassi
rulers.title: High priest and ethnarch
rulers.note: Assumed leadership in 143 BCE; recognised leader and high priest by decree in 141; assassinated 135 (infobox, February) or 134 (body) BCE.

rulers.name: John Hyrcanus I
rulers.title: High priest and ethnarch
rulers.note: Assumed leadership c. 135 BCE; the end year is the year before Aristobulus I's title of king (104-103); neither page gives his death year.

rulers.name: Aristobulus I
rulers.title: King
rulers.note: '104-103 BCE': takes the title of king and conquers Galilee.

rulers.name: Alexander Jannaeus
rulers.title: King
rulers.note: 'After a reign of 27 years, he died c. 76 BCE ... during the siege of Ragaba.'

rulers.name: Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II (rival claimants)
rulers.note: The brothers contest the throne 67-63; Pompey ends it by capturing Jerusalem in 63.

rulers.name: Hyrcanus II
rulers.title: High priest, ethnarch from 47
rulers.note: Pompey restored him as high priest without the royal title; Rome recognised him as ethnarch in 47 BCE; Antigonus displaced him in 40 (end year is the Hasmonean page's date for Antigonus's installation).

rulers.name: Antigonus II Mattathias
rulers.title: King
rulers.note: Installed as king by the Parthian army in 40 BCE; ends 37 when Herod defeats him.

rulers.name: Herod the Great
rulers.title: King (client of Rome)
rulers.note: Named King of the Jews by the Senate in 40 (Josephus; Appian 39); took Jerusalem 37 (Schürer) or 36 (Steinmann); died 4 BCE (Schürer) or 1 BCE (Steinmann).

rulers.name: Herod Archelaus
rulers.title: Ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea
rulers.note: Ethnarch 'until 6 CE', when Augustus removed him.

Fix fx-31 (F165): verdict ok -> adjust: Edom and the Negev south of Beersheba (shared with nabataeans, 12 and 19 cells) are subtracted as in judea_-91 and judea_-65; the Alexander Jannaeus page (opened 2026-11-01) mentions neither region.

the Hasmonean kingdom in year -66, before Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63, without Edom and the Negev south of Beersheba, which stay Nabataean (no page opened has Judea holding them; ledger -65 returns Moab)

correction.text: Judea in the succession war after the Nabataean towns went back: the Cliopatria shape without Moab, Edom and the Negev south of Beersheba, years -65 to -64

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for -65..-64, added in the repair pass so that the shape and ledger -65 agree (judea_-66 had kept the Nabataean cells for -66..-64 while the ledger lost them at -65). 68 of the shape's 109 cells remain. correction.text: Judea under Pompey's settlement: the Hasmonean maximum without the coastal plain, the Decapolis cities and the Nabataean towns returned during the succession war

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for -63..-50 (the Cliopatria shape of the same years is kept unchanged at 31.9k km2). 'The Hasmonean kingdom was forced to relinquish the coastal plain', losing Mediterranean access, along with parts of Idumea and Samaria; 'several Hellenistic cities gained autonomy as the Decapolis'. The page gives no boundaries, so the coast is three radii (Jaffa 20, Gaza 25, Caesarea 25 km), the Decapolis one radius at Gerasa (40 km, which also takes in Pella and Dium), and the Nabataean towns the Jannaeus page has recovered by negotiation with Hyrcanus II during the succession war (Moab, Edom, the Negev south of Beersheba) are removed as well (ledger -65, confidence 1). The parts of Idumea and Samaria are not subtracted for want of a boundary.

correction.text: the Cliopatria shape without the coastal plain, the Decapolis cities and the Nabataean towns (Pompey's settlement of 63), years -49 to -41

correction.text: the Cliopatria shape without the coastal plain, the Decapolis cities and the Nabataean towns, years -40 to -37 (Antigonus Mattathias, Parthian-backed)

keyframe_review.note: 31,920 km2 for -40..-37. Cliopatria's Parthian shape overlaps Judea's cells in these years (it holds Samaria, Galilee, Golan, Hauran cells), which no opened page explains.

correction.text: the Cliopatria shape without the coastal plain, the Decapolis cities and the Nabataean towns, years -36 to -28 (Herod's kingdom)

keyframe_review.note: 31,961 km2 for -36..-28. Herod's kingdom from 37; the Herodian kingdom infobox lists Judea, Idumea, Samaria, Galilee and several regions east of the Jordan River, and no area. correction.text: the Cliopatria shape without the coastal plain, the Decapolis cities and the Nabataean towns, years -27 to -26

The Judea page dates Herod's founding of Caesarea Maritima to c. 25 BCE and makes it the capital, so the coast at Caesarea is Herod's from then; how the rest of the coast (Jaffa, Gaza) came back is not on the pages opened (the Herodian kingdom page, reopened in the repair pass, is silent), and the ledger bridges it at -25 with confidence 1. Repair pass: the verdict was ok, which drew 41 Moab/Edom/Negev cells (lost to the Nabataeans at -65, ledger) and 9 Gerasa-district cells (lost to the Decapolis at -63, ledger) back for six years and omitted the Hauran grant; no ledger event regains them, so they are subtracted (59 cells). the northern Hauran: Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line; the line towns (Adraa, Bosra, Salkhad) and the Hauran south of them stay Nabataean

correction.text: Herod's kingdom with Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis (the northern Hauran) added in 22 BCE: the Cliopatria shape without Moab, Edom, the Negev south of Beersheba and the Gerasa district, plus the northern Hauran (Bosra and the southern Hauran stay Nabataean), years -22 to -20

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for -22..-20 (99 cells). 'In 22 BCE Augustus grants Herod the regions of Trachonitis, Batanaea, and Auranitis' (Herod the Great page, timeline); the Cliopatria -25 shape holds only 8 of the 45 Hauran cells. The Nabataean and Gerasa cells stay subtracted as in judea_-25. judea_-19 (from -19) has the same extent on the -19 base shape. Fix fx-31 (F165): the grant is the northern Hauran only. The Hauran page (opened 2026-11-01): 'The Arab Nabateans expanded their presence to the southern Hauran towns of Bosra and Salkhad'; the 106 provincial boundary 'followed the boundary just north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line', the line that 'had separated the Herodian and Nabatean kingdoms'; the Herod the Great page gives the grant only as 'Trachonitis, Batanaea, and Auranitis in the northeast'. So the Hauran north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line is Herod's (30 of 45 cells, with Trachonitis/Lajat and Batanaea/Nuqrah); the line towns and the Hauran south of them, and the Irbid (Gilead) cells, are subtracted. Review fx-31: an earlier version subtracted the Cliopatria Nabataean -64 shape and a 40 km Bosra disc, which removed Trachonitis and Batanaea, the core of the 22 BCE grant, and Suwayda/Auranitis north of the line; replaced by the line itself.

the northern Hauran: Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line; the line towns (Adraa, Bosra, Salkhad) and the Hauran south of them stay Nabataean

So the Hauran north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line is Herod's (30 of 45 cells, with Trachonitis/Lajat and Batanaea/Nuqrah); the line towns and the Hauran south of them, and the Irbid (Gilead) cells, are subtracted. correction.text: Archelaus's ethnarchy: Judea, Samaria and Idumea (the Judea region covers the Hebron hills; the Negev within 40 km of Beersheba is added as the south of Idumea), with the Caesarea coast

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for -4..5 (51 cells). At Herod's death 'Augustus respected the terms of Herod's will': Archelaus ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea until 6 CE; Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea; Philip tetrarch of Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis and Paneas. Caesarea Maritima is added because the Judaea page makes it the capital of the province that took over Archelaus's land. The tetrarchies leave the shape (ledger splits at -4). Repair pass: the Negev within 40 km of Beersheba (12 cells that the earlier shape dropped without an event) is added as the south of Idumea; the Idumea page puts Persian-period Idumea 'down to the area north of Be'er Sheva' and the Herodian kingdom page gives Archelaus 'Judea, Samaria and Idumea'. Four rim cells of the -19 shape (two at Amman, two on the coast plain) are in neither this shape nor the split regions and have no page: the Gaza, Gadara and Hippos cities' fate at Herod's death is not on the pages opened.

correction.text: Judea, Samaria and Idumea under Archelaus (to 6 CE) with the Caesarea coast and the Beersheba country; the same shape as judea_-4

keyframe_review.note: 31,921 km2 for 1..5. Replaced by judea_-4 (repair pass: now with the Beersheba country as the south of Idumea): Galilee, Peraea and the north-east are the tetrarchies of Antipas and Philip, not Judea. The province formed in 6 CE, a year after Cliopatria's last Judea year, from 'Judea, Samaria, and Idumea'; Galilee and Peraea were not added until 44 CE.

region.text: Judea around Jerusalem, with Jaffa and Gezer: independent from 142 BCE

ledger.note: 142: Demetrius II grants Judea tax exemption and with it recognises its independence under Simon. 'The fact that his request was granted implied recognition of the political independence of Judea in the year 142 BCE.' The page has Simon assuming leadership in 143 and securing Gezer and Jaffa; the Acra in Jerusalem was still Seleucid. The Judea page timeline dates Seleucid rule to 141 and the Hasmonean kingdom from 141; the Hasmonean page gives 142/141.

region.text: the Acra fortress in Jerusalem, the last Hellenistic presence in the city

ledger.note: 141: Simon takes the Acra, the last Seleucid fortress in Jerusalem. 'In 142/141 BCE, he captured the Acra fortress in Jerusalem'; the Hasmonean page has 'the citadel [Acra] in 141 BC'. In 141 the Jews decreed that Simon 'should be their leader and high priest forever'.

region.text: Judea under John Hyrcanus, a Seleucid tributary

ledger.note: 134: Judea becomes a Seleucid tributary. 'Antiochus VII Sidetes marched into Judea, pillaged the countryside, and laid what became a year-long siege of Jerusalem'; the truce required 'payment of 3,000 talents of silver to Antiochus', the dismantling of the walls, Judean participation in the Seleucid war against the Parthians and 'renewed Judean recognition of Seleucid control'. The page dates the siege only to Hyrcanus's first year (c. 134). Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of seleucid-empire /ledger/73, which carries the same event with Judea as counterpart).

region.text: Judea

ledger.note: 129: Judea stops paying tribute. 'After Antiochus VII's death in 129 BCE, Hyrcanus ceased tribute payments' (the page also gives 128 for the death). Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of seleucid-empire /ledger/78).

region.text: Idumea (Adora, Maresha) and the rest of the Judean hills and Shephelah in the Cliopatria -126 shape beyond the 144 core, Samaria and Medeba

ledger.note: Idumea and the southern hills join Judea under John Hyrcanus. The page says he conquered Adora, Maresha and other towns and forced the Idumeans to convert, with no year; the year is Cliopatria's (the -126 shape is 32 cells larger than -144). The Hasmonean page also gives Samaria and Idumea to Hyrcanus without a date. The previous holder is not named on the page (the Seleucid Empire is the neighbour in Cliopatria). Repair pass: the Idumea page, opened again, also gives no year; it quotes Josephus on Hyrcanus capturing 'the Idumean cities of Adora and Marisa' and 'subduing all the Idumeans', says Persian-period Idumea reached 'down to the area north of Be'er Sheva', and adds that since the late 1980s some scholars hold 'Idumaea was not annexed by the Hasmoneans at all'. The year stays Cliopatria's (confidence 1).

region.text: Samaria city and region

ledger.note: 113: Hyrcanus attacks Samaria. 'Beginning in 113 BCE, Hyrcanus began an extensive military campaign against Samaria.' The page does not say which state held the city; the Cliopatria Seleucid shape of the time holds about one Samaria cell. Counterpart nobody (repair pass): Samaria was an autonomous Hellenistic city and Samaritan community, not a state with a dossier; 'The Samaritans called for help and eventually received 6,000 troops from Antiochus IX Cyzicenus' is an ally's relief, and the seleucid-empire dossier carries no loss of Samaria.

region.text: Samaria with Shechem and Mount Gerizim

ledger.note: 110: Shechem and Mount Gerizim fall, then Samaria. 'This military action against Shechem has been dated archaeologically around 111–110 BCE'; Shechem was reduced to a village and the Samaritan Temple on Mount Gerizim destroyed; 'Ultimately Samaria was overrun and devastated' (undated). Counterpart nobody (repair pass), as for the 113 contest start.

region.text: Samaria

ledger.note: 110: the Samaria campaign ends with Shechem and Gerizim destroyed (111-110 per the page); the capture of Samaria city itself is undated. Counterpart nobody (repair pass), as for the 113 contest start.

region.text: Medeba in Transjordan

ledger.note: 110: Medeba falls to Hyrcanus, his first conquest east of the Jordan; the page has Medeba besieged and taken after six months. The page does not name its previous holder; Cliopatria's Nabataean shape holds 1-3 Madaba cells in these years.

region.text: Galilee

ledger.note: 103: Aristobulus I takes the royal title and conquers Galilee. The Hasmonean page dates both to 104-103 BCE ('103-76 BCE' then has Jannaeus conquering Iturea); the year is the later of the two. The Hasmonean page names no previous holder. Repair pass: the Ituraea page says 'In 105 BCE, Hasmonean leader Aristobulus I campaigned against Iturea' and annexed a large portion of it (a year earlier than the Hasmonean page's 104-103); the researcher reads the Iturean land as the north of Galilee, so the Itureans replace the Seleucid Empire as counterpart (Cliopatria's Seleucid shape holds 14 Galilee cells in -110 and 8 in -91, and the seleucid-empire dossier carries no loss of Galilee). The Itureans need a dossier.

region.text: Gaza

ledger.note: 96: Jannaeus takes Gaza. 'In 96 BCE, Jannaeus defeated the inhabitants of Gaza', which cut the Nabataeans off from direct access to the Mediterranean. The page names no state as ruler of Gaza.

region.text: the Moab cells added by the -91 shape

ledger.note: Jannaeus's reign adds the Negev, Edom and Moab margin from the Nabataeans (Cliopatria's step from -110 to -91). The Jannaeus page has Obodas I ambushing him near Gadara and defeating him in the Golan (undated) and calls Gaza's fall the blow to Nabataean sea access; it dates no gain in this land. The year is the shape's. Repair pass: the Obodas I page says 'Moab and Gilead, two mountainous areas east of the Dead Sea' which 'the Hasmoneans had conquered from the Nabataeans previously, were returned' (undated, after the clash near Gadara 'around 93 BC'), and does not mention Edom or the Negev. The nabataeans dossier dates the loss c. 96 and the regain c. 93; this dossier keeps Cliopatria's shape (the margin held -91 to -65) because the Jannaeus page has the Nabataeans recovering their cities 'only through negotiations with his elder son, Hyrcanus II'. The two dossiers disagree on the Moab years and no page opened settles it. Fix fx-31 (F165): narrowed to Moab. The Alexander Jannaeus page (opened 2026-11-01) says Alexander 'returned the land he had seized in Moab and Galaaditis from the Nabataeans' (undated) and has no sentence on Edom or the Negev, so those two are no longer gained (the Nabataean dossier carries them throughout).

region.text: Gaulanitis and Galaaditis

ledger.note: 83: Jannaeus campaigns east of the Jordan. 'From 83 to 80 BCE, Alexander continued campaigning in the east'; Aretas III defeated him near Adida, after which Josephus says they reached an agreement.

region.text: Golan, Seleucia and Gamala in Gaulanitis

ledger.note: 80: Jannaeus takes Golan, Seleucia and Gamala in Gaulanitis. 'Alexander then took Golan, Seleucia, and Gamala in Gaulanitis.' The page names no previous holder; Cliopatria's Seleucid shape holds Golan cells until -110. Repair pass: the Ituraea page, opened for this, says only that Iturean settlement expanded into the Golan after the Seleucid collapse (undated), so the holder in 83-80 may have been Seleucid, Iturean or Armenian; no page opened names it, and the Seleucid Empire stays as the Cliopatria neighbour.

region.text: Pella, Dium and Gerasa in Galaaditis

ledger.note: 80: Jannaeus takes Pella, Dium and Gerasa in Galaaditis (he destroyed Pella). The page names no previous holder; the Nabataeans are the neighbour.

region.text: Gaulanitis and Galaaditis

ledger.note: 80: the eastern campaign ends with the cities taken (83-80 per the page).

region.text: Moab, the land the Jannaeus page has returned to the Nabataeans

ledger.note: The Nabataean towns go back. The Jannaeus page says Alexander later returned land in 'Moab and Galaaditis' to the Nabataeans (undated) and, in the page's words as read, that Nabataean cities were recovered through negotiations with Hyrcanus II during the succession war (67-63); -65 is the middle of that war and the year is the researcher's. Galaaditis is left in the shape because the Herodian pages give Herod regions east of the Jordan. Repair pass: the Aretas III page (opened again) dates Hyrcanus II's accession to 67, has Aretas 'besieging the city for several months' and Hyrcanus's allies returning 'the Arabian towns taken by the Hasmoneans', all undated, and puts the Roman march on Petra in 62; -65 stays the researcher's year (confidence 1) and judea_-65 now carries the shape from that year. Fix fx-31 (F165): narrowed to Moab, since Edom and the Negev south of Beersheba are no longer in Judea's shapes (see ledger -91); the Alexander Jannaeus page has Alexander return the land seized 'in Moab and Galaaditis'.

63: Pompey takes Jerusalem and ends the Hasmonean kingship. Pompey restored Hyrcanus as high priest but removed his royal title; Judea stays autonomous but tributary, 'a client kingdom of the Roman Republic'. The dynasty and the state continue; colour is kept.

region.text: the coastal plain: Jaffa, Gaza, the Caesarea coast

ledger.note: 63: the coastal plain goes. 'The Hasmonean kingdom was forced to relinquish the coastal plain', losing Mediterranean access. The page does not say who received it, only that Judea became dependent on the Roman administration in Syria; the Roman Republic is the counterpart. The radii are the researcher's.

region.text: the Decapolis cities in the Gerasa district

ledger.note: 63: Hellenistic cities become autonomous. Several Hellenistic cities gained autonomy as the Decapolis (the page's words as read). The page does not list the cities; the Gerasa-Pella-Dium district (taken by Jannaeus in 83-80) is used. Parts of Idumea and Samaria also went (undated boundary, not drawn). Counterpart roman-republic (repair pass): 'Several Hellenistic cities were granted autonomy to form the Decapolis' (the page's words, reopened); the page does not say who governed them, only that Judea 'became dependent on the Roman administration in Syria', so the Roman Republic that Pompey acted for is the counterpart; the Decapolis is no state with a dossier.

region.text: Judea under Hyrcanus II after Pompey's settlement

ledger.note: 63: Judea becomes a client of Rome. 'Judea remained autonomous but was obliged to pay tribute and became dependent on the Roman administration in Syria'; the page speaks of 'the incorporation of Judea as a client kingdom of the Roman Republic'. Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-republic /ledger/171).

47: Rome recognises Hyrcanus II as ethnarch. the Siege of Jerusalem page has Rome later recognising Hyrcanus as ethnarch in 47 BC; the Hasmonean page has him 'restored as ethnarch' in 47. The state is an ethnarchy under Roman tribute.

40: the Parthians install Antigonus as king. A Parthian army crosses the Euphrates, Antigonus is installed as king, and the Senate names Herod King of the Jews (Hasmonean dynasty page). The Parthian dossier should carry the client relation; Judea's land is not stated.

region.text: Judea under Hyrcanus II until the Parthian invasion

ledger.note: 40: the Roman client relation ends when the Parthians install Antigonus. A Parthian army crosses the Euphrates and installs Antigonus as king while the Senate names Herod King of the Jews (Hasmonean dynasty page). Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-republic /ledger/193).

region.text: Judea under Antigonus Mattathias, installed by the Parthian army

ledger.note: 40: Antigonus is installed as king by a Parthian army. The page says 'installed' and does not call the kingdom a client; the client reading is the researcher's. The parthian-empire dossier (group me-06, not yet written) should carry the mirror.

37: Herod defeats Antigonus and ends Hasmonean rule; the Herodian client kingdom of Rome begins. 'Herod was victorious over his rival in 37 BCE.' The Herod the Great page dates the siege to 'the summer of 37 BCE' (Schürer) or 36 BCE (Steinmann); the Senate had named him king in 40 (Appian: 39).

region.text: Judea under Antigonus Mattathias

ledger.note: 37: Herod defeats Antigonus and ends the Parthian-backed Hasmonean kingship ('Herod was victorious over his rival in 37 BCE', Herodian kingdom page; 36 per Steinmann on the Herod the Great page).

region.text: Judea under Herod, client king of Rome

ledger.note: 37: Judea is a Roman client kingdom again under Herod. 'Herod was victorious over his rival in 37 BCE' (Herodian kingdom page); 'Herod ruled Judaea as a client kingdom of Rome until his death in 4 BCE' (Judaea (Roman province) page). Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-republic /ledger/199).

region.text: Judea under Herod

ledger.note: 27: the client relation passes from the Republic to the Empire. The roman-republic and roman-empire dossiers date the end of the Republic and the start of the Empire to January 27 BCE; the pages opened give no separate act for Judea ('Rome maintained a system of semi-autonomous vassalage in the region', Judaea (Roman province) page). Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-republic's dissolution).

region.text: Judea under Herod

ledger.note: 27: Judea is a client kingdom of the Roman Empire. 'Herod ruled Judaea as a client kingdom of Rome until his death in 4 BCE', then the ethnarchy of Archelaus until his dismissal; the tetrarchies of 4 BCE were clients too. Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-empire /ledger/2).

c. 25: Herod founds Caesarea Maritima and makes it the capital. 'c. 25 BCE: Caesarea Maritima is built by Herod the Great, replacing Jerusalem as the capital.' The Herodian kingdom page still lists Jerusalem as capital.

region.text: the coastal plain Pompey detached in 63, Caesarea, Jaffa and Gaza

ledger.note: The coastal plain is Herod's again. The page has Herod building Caesarea Maritima c. 25 BCE, so the coast at Caesarea is his; the return of Jaffa and Gaza is not on the pages opened (the Herod the Great page says only that Octavian 'confirms him as King of Judea at Rhodes' in 30). The year is the Judea page's Caesarea date; the Cliopatria shape includes the whole coast from -25. Repair pass: the Herodian kingdom page, opened again, does not mention Actium or any grant of Gaza, Jaffa or the coastal cities (the Herod the Great page is silent too); the event stays a confidence-1 bridge.

union.text: the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line and the Hauran south of it: the boundary runs about 6 km north of Adraa (Daraa), Bosra and Salkhad

region.text: the northern Hauran: Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line; the line towns (Adraa, Bosra, Salkhad) and the Hauran south of them stay Nabataean

ledger.note: 22: Augustus gives Herod Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis. The Herod the Great page dates the grant of Trachonitis, Batanaea and Auranitis to 22 BCE (not 23 or 20). The giver is Augustus; the page does not say whose land it had been, so the Roman Empire is the counterpart. Fix fx-31 (F165): the region is the northern Hauran only; the Hauran page (opened 2026-11-01) has the Nabataeans in the southern Hauran towns of Bosra and Salkhad and the later Roman boundary just north of the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line, 'the boundary' between the Herodian and Nabatean kingdoms; the Hauran page dates the transfer 23 BC, the Herod the Great page 22 BCE (kept). Review fx-31: the subtraction is now the Adraa-Bosra-Salkhad line and the Hauran south of it (polygon) plus the Irbid (Gilead) cells, not the Cliopatria Nabataean -64 shape (which held Trachonitis and Batanaea, the land granted) and a 40 km Bosra disc.

4: Herod dies and his kingdom is divided; Archelaus holds the ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea. 'Herod died in 4 BCE, and his kingdom was divided among his three sons' (Herodian kingdom page; the Herod the Great page gives 4 BCE (Schürer) or 1 BCE (Steinmann)). Augustus respected the terms of Herod's will.

region.text: Galilee and Peraea

ledger.note: 4: Antipas becomes tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea, from Herod's death 'to 39 CE when he was deposed and exiled'. Peraea has no gazetteer entry, Gilead (Galaaditis) is used.

region.text: Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis and Paneas

ledger.note: 4: Philip becomes tetrarch of Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis and Paneas, ruling until his death in 34 CE. Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea and Paneas have no gazetteer entries; Golan and Hauran are used.

region.text: Archelaus's Judea, Samaria and Idumea

ledger.note: 6 CE: Archelaus is dismissed and the client ethnarchy is annexed. 'He was dismissed in 6 CE by the first Roman emperor, Augustus, after an appeal from his own subjects'; 'Following his removal, Judaea was annexed as the Roman province of Judaea'. Judea is the vassal and the counterpart is the suzerain (mirror of roman-empire /ledger/22).

region.text: Judea, Samaria and Idumea (with the Beersheba country as the south of Idumea)

ledger.note: 6 CE: Augustus deposes Archelaus and Judea becomes a Roman province. 'The province's formal incorporation into the Roman Empire was enacted by Augustus in 6 AD'; Quirinius's census 'conducted ... in 6 CE' triggered the revolt of Judas of Galilee; Coponius was the first prefect. 'Judea, Samaria, and Idumea came under direct Roman administration.' Repair pass: the Beersheba country is added to the region as the south of Idumea (the Judaea page names Judea, Samaria and Idumaea, 'the domains previously ruled by Herod Archelaus').

wars.name: Siege of Jerusalem by Antiochus VII
wars.outcome: Antiochus VII besieged Jerusalem for a year (from Hyrcanus's first regnal year) and imposed 3,000 talents of silver, the dismantling of the walls, Judean help in the Parthian war and renewed Seleucid recognition; after Antiochus VII's death (129 or 128, the page gives both) Hyrcanus 'ceased tribute payments' and acted independently.
wars.note: Judea was a Seleucid tributary in these years; the vassal event belongs in the seleucid-empire dossier. The page does not date the end of the siege.

wars.name: John Hyrcanus's Samaria and Transjordan campaigns
wars.outcome: Hyrcanus overran and devastated Samaria (Shechem a village, the Gerizim temple destroyed, 111-110) and took Medeba after a six-month siege in 110.
wars.note: The page does not name the opponents of the Samaria campaign or the holder of Medeba.

wars.name: Wars of Alexander Jannaeus with Gaza and the Nabataeans
wars.outcome: Gaza fell in 96; Obodas I ambushed Alexander near Gadara and beat him in the Golan (undated); Aretas III defeated him near Adida, after which they agreed terms (83-80); Alexander then took Golan, Seleucia, Gamala, Pella, Dium and Gerasa and later gave Moab and Galaaditis back.
wars.note: Only 96 and 83-80 are dated on the page; 'c. 93 BCE' for the ambush is not on it.

wars.name: Hasmonean civil war and Pompey's capture of Jerusalem
wars.outcome: Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II contested the throne; Pompey took Jerusalem after a three-month siege in 63, restored Hyrcanus as high priest without the royal title, took Aristobulus to Rome and dismembered the kingdom (coastal plain relinquished, Decapolis cities autonomous).
wars.note: The page gives no month. Aristobulus II and Hyrcanus II's battle near Jericho is undated on the Hasmonean page.

wars.name: Parthian invasion and Herod's reconquest of Judea
wars.outcome: A Parthian army installed Antigonus as king in 40 while the Senate named Herod King of the Jews; Herod, helped by Rome, defeated Antigonus in 37 (36 per Steinmann) and ended Hasmonean rule.
wars.note: The Herod the Great page: 'Herod and Sosius set out with a large army in 37 or 36 BCE'.

wars.name: Herod's Nabataean war
wars.outcome: The Herod the Great page's timeline: '32 BCE - The Nabatean war begins, with victory one year later'; no land is named. It also places a war against the Nabataeans at c. 10 BCE and a quarrel with Augustus in 9 BCE over its course.
wars.note: No territorial result on the page, so no zone.

wars.name: Revolt after Herod's death
wars.outcome: A messianic revolt followed Herod's death and was crushed by Varus, who crucified about 2,000 rebels (Judaea page).

certainty.note: Hasmonean, Roman-settlement and Herodian frontiers are approximate: the pages name cities and regions, never boundaries. No survey or treaty line is given for any of the borders; the 63 BCE cuts and the 4 BCE partition are the pages' regions drawn as radii.

notes:
Phase B, group me-05-f, state judea. Nine pages opened (the page budget): Judea, Hasmonean dynasty, John Hyrcanus, Alexander Jannaeus, Siege of Jerusalem (63 BC), Herodian kingdom, Herod the Great, Judaea (Roman province), Simon Thassi. None of them gives an area, so no infobox comparison is possible for any shape; verdict notes say so.

Cliopatria row: one 'Judea' row -144..5, 13 shapes. The shapes are coarse: -144 (20 cells), -126 (52), -110 (54), -91 (110) and then 109-114 cells unchanged to 5, so Pompey's settlement of 63, Herod's kingdom, the 22 BCE grant and the 4 BCE partition are not drawn. The dossier corrects with four new keyframes (judea_-65, judea_-63, judea_-22 and judea_-4) and splits judea_-66, judea_-25 and judea_-19 by years. The row ends 5; the province forms 6 CE, so identity.end is 6.

Start: Cliopatria -144; the pages give 142 (Simon page: recognition of independence), 142/141 (Hasmonean dynasty) and 141 (Judea page timeline: Hasmonean kingdom 141-37). identity.start is -142.

Disagreements between pages: Antiochus VII's death 129 vs 128 (John Hyrcanus page, both); Herod's siege of Jerusalem summer 37 (Schürer) vs 36 (Steinmann); Herod's death 4 BCE vs 1 BCE; Simon's death 135 (infobox) vs 134; Herod named king 40 (Josephus) vs 39 (Appian); capital Jerusalem (Herodian kingdom infobox) vs Caesarea Maritima from c. 25 (Judea page). The Jannaeus page does not support the 'c. 93 BCE' date for the Nabataean ambush; Gaza 96 and the 83-80 campaign are the only dated items.

Not settled (page silent), in order of weight: (1) the Idumea conquest year under Hyrcanus I (event -126, confidence 1, year from the Cliopatria shape); (2) the Negev/Edom/Moab margin the -91 shape draws (event -91, confidence 1) and the date it went back to the Nabataeans (event -65, confidence 1, middle of the succession war the Jannaeus page names); (3) the grants after Actium (30 BCE) that returned the coast to Herod: only Caesarea c. 25 is on the pages, so the coastal gain at -25 is confidence 1; (4) Gabinius's division into five districts in 57 BCE (Judea page) changes no border and has no event type, so it is not in the ledger; (5) the parts of Idumea and Samaria Pompey detached are on the Siege of Jerusalem page without boundaries and are not subtracted; (6) the owner of Medeba, Galilee and Golan before the Hasmoneans (counterparts nabataeans/seleucid-empire are read from Cliopatria shapes, not from the pages); (7) the land Antigonus held in 40-37.

Status events: the Seleucid tribute 134-129, the Roman client years (63-40 and 37-27 Republic, 27 BCE-6 CE Empire) and Antigonus's Parthian backing (40-37) are vassal_start/vassal_end events here (repair pass), with the suzerain as counterpart; the schema words the counterpart of a vassal event as the vassal itself, so these are the vassal's side of the suzerain's own events (seleucid-empire /ledger/73 and /78, roman-republic /ledger/171, 193 and 199, roman-empire /ledger/2 and 22) and must not be drawn twice. The parthian-empire dossier (me-06, not yet written) should carry the mirror of the 40-37 pair.

New states needed: the tetrarchies of 4 BCE. 'Tetrarchy of Galilee and Peraea' (Herod Antipas, -4..39 per the Herod the Great page) and 'Tetrarchy of Philip' (Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Paneas, -4..34): referenced as counterparts in the -4 split events with the slugs tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea and tetrarchy-of-philip; they are Roman clients (rule 4 tint). The repair pass uses roman-republic as counterpart of the 63 Decapolis loss and nobody for Samaria (113-110); it names the Itureans (itureans) as counterpart of the Galilee gain of 103 and lists them as a state needing a dossier.

Overlaps with other dossiers: Cliopatria's Nabataean shape holds Edom (43) and Negev (14) cells while the Judea shape draws them (-91 to 5); Cliopatria's Roman Republic/Empire and Parthian shapes overlap Judea's Galilee, Golan and Hauran cells in 63-5. This dossier's corrections remove the Nabataean cells from -65, the coast and the Gerasa district from 63 (coast back from -25, Gerasa not returned); the Galilee/Golan/Hauran overlaps remain because the pages do not say the Romans or Parthians held them.

Gazetteer: no entries for Peraea, Decapolis, Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Paneas or Gezer; Gilead stands in for Peraea/Galaaditis, Golan and Hauran for Philip's tetrarchy, and Jaffa for Gezer. The 'Edom' region carries Idumea as an alias but is the Nabataean Edom south of the Dead Sea, not Hyrcanus's Idumea around Hebron; this dossier uses 'Judea' (which covers the Hebron hills) for Idumea proper.

Repair pass 2026-10-19 (reviewer's findings on judea): (1) judea_-25 is now adjust (59 cells: Moab, Edom, the Negev south of Beersheba and the Gerasa district removed) with a new keyframe judea_-22 adding the Hauran (99 cells), and judea_-19 subtracts the Gerasa district too. (2) New judea_-65 limits judea_-66 to one year so that the shape and the -65 loss agree. (3) Ten vassal events added (Seleucid -134/-129; Roman Republic -63/-40 and -37/-27; Parthian -40/-37; Roman Empire -27/6). (4) The Beersheba country (Negev within 40 km) is added to judea_-4, judea_1 and the 6 CE region as Idumea's south; four rim cells (two at Amman, two on the coast plain) have no page. (5) Counterparts: Decapolis -> roman-republic, Samaria -> nobody, Galilee 103 -> itureans. Pages opened again: Aretas III, Obodas I, Idumea, Ituraea, Herodian kingdom, Siege of Jerusalem (63 BC), John Hyrcanus, Judaea (Roman province). Not settled by them: the Idumea year (-126), the date Moab left (the Obodas I page has Moab and Gilead returned after c. 93, undated; this dossier keeps Cliopatria's margin to -65, against the nabataeans dossier's c. 93), the post-Actium coastal grants, and the holder of the Golan in 83-80. The Siege of Jerusalem page does not say who governed the Decapolis cities; the roman-republic counterpart is the researcher's reading.
